content: The lifetime risk of HIV infection among sex workers is significantly higher compared to the general population. This elevated risk is attributed to several factors, including having multiple sexual partners, unsafe working conditions, limited ability to negotiate consistent condom use, lack of access to appropriate lubricants, high prevalence of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and the sharing of injecting equipment. Sex workers are five times more likely to acquire HIV than other women aged 15–49 years, even in countries with high HIV prevalence. Sex workers often lack control over these risk factors due to the environments and contexts in which they live and work. Consequently, they are considered a key population for targeted interventions to curb the HIV epidemic. Their high rates of partner change and unsafe work environments expose them to frequent infections and increase their risk of HIV acquisition, which can subsequently be transmitted to their clients, including those who are highly mobile. These clients, in turn, may spread the infection to other sexual partners. Sex workers’ autonomy and ability to protect their health are influenced by varying levels of financial security, diverse work settings, and conditions. In many contexts, stigma, discrimination, criminalization, violence, financial need, debt, and exploitation further exacerbate their vulnerability. Therefore, it is crucial to understand the contexts of sex work, the surrounding power structures, and the broader health and social needs of sex workers when designing interventions. Effective interventions with sex workers are a critical component of comprehensive HIV prevention and treatment strategies. Evidence shows that targeted HIV prevention programs aimed at reducing HIV/STI transmission among sex workers are both feasible and effective. However, many of these programs have had limited impact on HIV transmission dynamics because they are implemented on a small and localized scale, leaving most sex workers unreached. Additionally, certain groups, such as male and transgender sex workers, are often overlooked. Addressing this prevention gap is a major challenge in HIV prevention among sex workers. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued guidance on the use of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in serodiscordant couples and men who have sex with men. Interventions to reduce HIV transmission among sex workers and their clients are recognized as essential components of HIV programming. Global experience suggests that effective sex worker interventions share common elements, but guidance on what constitutes effective HIV programming in the context of sex work remains scarce. This gap hinders the scaling up of interventions, as called for in universal access targets. In the absence of globally recognized guidelines, countries often have to improvise, leading to inefficiencies. Five years ago, the WHO HIV Department attempted to address this gap by publishing the HIV/AIDS sex work toolkit, which compiled known guidelines and training materials from different regions. In response to new experiences and the need for evidence, countries have requested WHO and UNAIDS to develop evidence-based guidance for designing, implementing, and monitoring effective HIV and STI prevention and treatment interventions among female, male, and transgender sex workers. The objective of this document is to provide technical recommendations on the prevention and treatment of HIV and other STIs among sex workers and their clients. These guidelines are intended for use by national public health officials, managers of HIV/AIDS and STI programs, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), community and civil society organizations, and health workers. They may also be of interest to international funding agencies, the scientific media, health policymakers, and advocates. Sex workers include female, male, and transgender adults and young people (18 years and older) who receive money or goods in exchange for sexual services, either regularly or occasionally. It is important to note that sex work involves consensual sex between adults and takes many forms, varying between and within countries and communities. Sex work may also differ in its degree of formality or organization. These guidelines include technical recommendations for designing a basic package of health interventions and services for the prevention and treatment of HIV and other STIs among sex workers and their clients. Although the focus is on lowand middle-income countries, the recommendations may also be applicable to sex workers in high-income countries. Effective HIV prevention requires scaling up multiple interventions that work synergistically to achieve maximum public health impact. Scaling up HIV prevention means ensuring that an appropriate mix of evidence-based prevention strategies achieves sufficient coverage, uptake, intensity, and duration to have an optimal public health effect. However, there is no one size fits all approach, and programs need to be tailored to local situations. WHO and UNAIDS are working with regional and country offices and partners to disseminate these evidence-based global guidelines and support regional and country adaptation, considering operational considerations and implementation methods appropriate to the local context of sex work and the capacity of health systems. WHO follows the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach for developing and reviewing recommendations. This approach is increasingly adopted worldwide for rating the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations. GRADE emphasizes a structured, explicit, and transparent approach to grading and consensus building. It separates the rating of evidence quality from the grading of recommendations. The quality of evidence reflects the confidence that the estimates of effect are adequate to support a particular recommendation. GRADE classifies evidence quality into four levels: high, moderate, low, and very low. The strength of a recommendation reflects the extent to which the desirable effects of an intervention outweigh the undesirable effects. GRADE classifies recommendations into two strengths: strong and conditional. Recommendations can also be either in favor of or against the intervention of interest, resulting in four combinations of strength and direction: strong in favor, conditional in favor, conditional against, and strong against. The WHO HIV Department led the development of these guidelines under the oversight of the WHO Guideline Review Committee (GRC) in collaboration with WHO’s Department of Reproductive Health and Research, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), UNAIDS Secretariat, and the Global Network of Sex Work Projects (NSWP). The process included identifying Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome (PICO) questions, conducting systematic reviews, and developing GRADE evidence tables. A technical meeting was held to monitor progress, and a qualitative survey on sex workers’ values and preferences was conducted by NSWP. Sex workers are entitled to the full protection of their human rights, as specified in international human rights instruments. These rights include non-discrimination, security of person and privacy, recognition and equality before the law, due process, the highest attainable standard of health, employment, just and favorable conditions of employment, peaceful assembly and association, freedom from arbitrary arrest and detention, and protection from violence. Laws that criminalize or penalize sex workers, their clients, and third parties, as well as abusive law enforcement practices, stigma, and discrimination, can undermine the effectiveness of HIV and sexual health programs and limit sex workers’ ability to access these programs. Violence against sex workers, repressive police practices, and stigma in healthcare settings are of particular concern. Sex worker-led organizations are crucial for enabling sex workers to protect themselves from discrimination, coercion, and violence. Measures that prevent them from organizing are also of significant concern.
